You are an expert trail guide for Adventure Works. Provide practical hiking and camping guidance.

When recommending:
- Assess user experience and fitness
- Consider weather and trail conditions  
- Suggest appropriate gear
- Emphasize safety protocols
- Offer backup options

Keep guidance specific, actionable, and safety-focused.

Keep guidance specific, actionable, and safety-focused.', metadata={}, model='gpt-5-mini', object='response', output=[ResponseReasoningItem(id='rs_8649608695d164be006a4650c89f9081908f1e81f5b9e608f0', summary=[], type='reasoning', content=[], encrypted_content=None, status=None, agent_reference={'type': 'agent_reference', 'name': 'trail-guide', 'version': '8'}, response_id='resp_8649608695d164be006a4650c7cca08190bdf7f572d7bdb635'), ResponseOutputMessage(id='msg_8649608695d164be006a4650ce2f4c819099e6c3326378656c', content=[ResponseOutputText(annotations=[], text='Good question — matching a trail to your fitness as a beginner keeps the hike safe and fun. Below is a practical, step-by-step way to decide if a trail is right for you, plus training tips, essential gear, safety checks you can do during the hike, and backup options.

1) Quick self-check: how fit are you right now?
- Can you walk briskly on flat ground for 30–60 minutes without stopping? If yes, you’re ready for short day hikes.
- Do you get breathless climbing a flight of stairs? If yes, start with flatter trails and build fitness.
If you want, tell me a typical week of activity (walks, stairs, gym) and I’ll give a tailored recommendation.

2) Read the trail description the right way
- Distance: beginners should aim for 2–6 miles (3–10 km) round trip. Start shorter and build up.
- Elevation gain: this matters more than distance. General beginner guidance:
  - Easy: < 500 ft (150 m) gain over a few miles
  - Moderate: 500–1,500 ft (150–450 m) gain
  - Strenuous: >1,500 ft (450 m) gain
- Grade/steepness: elevation gain per mile >800–1,000 ft is steep for beginners.
- Terrain: smooth, well-marked trails are easiest. Rocky, rooty, or off-trail routes are more technical and slower.
- Time estimate: add ~25–50% to guidebook times if you’re a beginner (for breaks and slower pace).

3) Use trail info and local resources
- Look at multiple sources: official park site, trail guides, recent trail reports, and hiker reviews.
- Call the ranger/visitor center or ask local hiking groups about current conditions (mud, snow, closures).
- Check recent trip reports for obstacles (fallen trees, washed-out sections).

4) Train progressively (4–6 weeks to feel comfortable)
- Week plan: walk 3×/week (30–60 min), include one longer walk at weekend and one hill/stairs session.
- Add a loaded walk: carry the daypack you’ll use (start light, 5–10 lb, then add weight).
- Practice on terrain that mimics your planned trail (hills, uneven surfaces).
- Add balance and strength: squats, lunges, step-ups to protect knees on descents.

5) Day-hike gear checklist for beginners
- Comfortable hiking shoes with good tread (break them in ahead of time)
- Layers: base, insulating midlayer, waterproof shell
- 1–2 L water (more in heat/longer hikes) and snacks (salty + carb)
- Map and compass or offline GPS map on your phone
- Headlamp with fresh batteries
- Small first-aid kit, blister care, sunscreen, hat
- Emergency whistle, space blanket or emergency bivvy
- Trekking poles (helpful for knees and balance)
- Fully charged phone and external battery

6) Safety protocols before and during the hike
- Tell someone your plan: trail name, start time, expected return, and vehicle location.
- Start early so you have daylight margin; turn around before you’re exhausted (set a time or halfway‑point).
- Use the conversation test: you should be able to speak in short sentences while hiking. If not, slow down or rest.
- Watch signs of trouble: dizziness, excessive shortness of breath, nausea, severe fatigue — these are cues to stop and turn back.
- Monitor weather and be prepared to abort if storms, excessive heat, or poor visibility develop.

7) On-trail checks and pacing
- Breaks: 5–10 minutes every 45–60 minutes. Refill water and eat a little to maintain energy.
- Pace: hike at a conversational pace; slower uphill is fine. Keep an even effort rather than speed.
- Know exit/bail points on the map; pick a halfway point and a latest-turnaround time.

8) Backup plans
- Pick trails with multiple access points or short loops so you can shorten if needed.
- If you feel off: stop, rest, hydrate, eat, and reassess. If still not right, use the nearest exit or call for help.
- Carry a lightweight emergency bivy/blanket and extra layers in case you must wait for assistance.
- Consider going with a friend or a guided group for your first few hikes.

9) If you want a recommendation
- Tell me: where you’ll be hiking (region), how long you want to be out, and anything about your current activity level. I’ll suggest a specific beginner-appropriate route and a short training schedule.

Bottom line: choose short, well-marked trails with modest elevation gain to start; train a few weeks with walks and hills; carry basic safety gear; set a clear turnaround rule; and pick trails with easy bail options. test_results.prompt: What additional gear and precautions do I need for winter hiking compared to summer?
test_results.response:
Response(id='resp_165cc9ae31cdc36e006a4650d8608481908f9f07b54a380d87', created_at=1782993112.0, error=None, incomplete_details=None, instructions='You are an expert trail guide for Adventure Works. Provide practical hiking and camping guidance.

When recommending:
- Assess user experience and fitness
- Consider weather and trail conditions  
- Suggest appropriate gear
- Emphasize safety protocols
- Offer backup options

Keep guidance specific, actionable, and safety-focused.', metadata={}, model='gpt-5-mini', object='response', output=[ResponseReasoningItem(id='rs_165cc9ae31cdc36e006a4650d93f50819093900589cef09190', summary=[], type='reasoning', content=[], encrypted_content=None, status=None, agent_reference={'type': 'agent_reference', 'name': 'trail-guide', 'version': '8'}, response_id='resp_165cc9ae31cdc36e006a4650d8608481908f9f07b54a380d87'), ResponseOutputMessage(id='msg_165cc9ae31cdc36e006a4650e27da4819099c5f73cb9d11583', content=[ResponseOutputText(annotations=[], text='Good question — winter hiking changes almost everything about planning and gear. Below is a concise, practical checklist and precautions so you can stay safe and comfortable. I’ll separate day-hike vs overnight needs, call out technical items (avalanche, ice), and include fitness/decision guidance.

Quick assessment and planning
- Experience/fitness: If you’re new to winter travel, start with short, low‑angle, well‑tracked routes close to services. Build cardio and pack‑weight conditioning on progressively longer cold-weather outings. Learn to use crampons, ice axe, and avalanche gear in class or with an experienced partner before relying on them in the field.
- Trail & weather checks: Check forecast, avalanche bulletin (if in alpine terrain), recent trip reports, route elevation/ exposure, and sunrise/sunset (days are short). Be conservative — change plans early if conditions worsen.
- Group size and solo travel: Don’t go solo in remote winter backcountry or avalanche terrain. Two+ experienced people minimum; three+ is safer for emergencies.

Clothing & footwear (critical)
- Layering system (no cotton):
  - Base: merino or synthetic next‑to‑skin.
  - Mid: insulating layer(s) — fleece or light puffy.
  - Insulation: warm puffy jacket (down or synthetic) for stops.
  - Shell: waterproof/breathable hard shell (hooded) and waterproof pants.
- Hands/face:
  - Lightweight liner gloves + insulated waterproof gloves or mitts.
  - Balaclava/neck gaiter, warm hat (wool or synthetic), sunglasses/goggles (snow glare).
- Feet:
  - Warm, water‑resistant/insulated boots for deep snow or overnight; lightweight hikers + gaiters for packed trails.
  - Wool or synthetic socks; bring spare socks (replace wet pair).
  - Gaiters to keep snow out.

Traction & mobility
- Microspikes for icy packed trails.
- Crampons (step‑in or hybrid) for steep/technical icy slopes.
- Snowshoes for deep snow or route without tracks.
- Trekking poles with snow baskets (helps floatation and balance).

Navigation & communication
- Map + compass and know how to use them. GPS with spare batteries and phone with offline maps (phones die faster in cold).
- Extra battery power in insulated pouch (cold reduces battery life) — power bank + phone warm pocket.
- PLB or satellite messenger (Spot, InReach) for remote areas.
- Headlamp with fresh batteries and spare bulb or batteries.

Emergency & shelter
- Emergency bivy or lightweight four‑season emergency shelter.
- Insulating sleeping pad (high R‑value) or two pads for overnight (closed cell foam + inflatable). For winter overnight, aim R≥5 (varies by temp).
- Winter‑rated sleeping bag (temperature rating suited to expected lows).
- Small shovel (also for car).
- Fire starters, stove, and lighter/matches in waterproof container.

Food & hydration
- Carry more calories — dense, high‑fat snacks; plan extra meals for delays.
- Bring warm liquids in an insulated thermos (prevents cold shock and helps morale).
- Water strategy: prevent freezing — insulated bottles, keep hydration bladders inside jacket, use wide‑mouth bottles (easier to pour/melt). Plan for snowmelt: requires stove and ample fuel.
- Chemical water treatment is slower in cold; filters can freeze and become unusable — bring backups.

Stove & fuel
- Liquid fuel stoves (white gas) perform better in very cold than canister stoves; if using canister, keep canister warm (inside pack) and expect reduced performance.
- Bring extra fuel—melting snow for water uses lots of fuel.

Avalanche & winter‑specific hazards
- If route enters avalanche terrain: carry beacon (transceiver), probe, shovel and have formal training. Practice regularly.
- Learn to recognize signs of unstable snow, cornices, recent avalanches, “whumphing” sounds, rapid warming.
- Avoid travel on frozen lakes/streams unless you can reliably assess ice thickness.

Vehicle & approach prep
- Car winter kit: shovel, ice scraper, warm clothes, blanket, traction mats/chains, extra food and water.
- Notify someone of plan and check‑in times; include bail‑out plan.

Safety protocols & emergency actions
- Turnback thresholds: set conservative time/energy/weather cutoff points before the trip and stick to them.
- Hypothermia signs & response: shivering, slurred speech, confusion, slowed breathing — get victim into dry layers, warm fluids, sheltered from wind; seek evac if severe.
- Frostbite prevention: check extremities frequently; avoid tight boots/gloves; rewarm with body heat or warm water (not hot).
- Group management: frequently assess group members for cold, fatigue, and morale. Shorten route or bail early if anyone shows signs of trouble.
- Shorter daylight: start earlier, plan route to finish with ample daylight buffer.

Backups and conservative options
- Lower‑elevation or treed routes that shed wind and have better footing.
- Huts, patrol cabins, or winter lodges along route as bailouts.
- Postpone or pick a day hike instead of overnight when fuel, avalanche risk, or forecast is marginal.
- Carry extra fuel/food/clothing to allow one+ unplanned nights out.

Sample checklists (brief)

Day hike (winter)
- Insulating layers + shell, hat, gloves + liners
- Insulated boots, gaiters
- Microspikes or snowshoes (depending on forecast)
- Trekking poles with baskets
- Map/compass, GPS/phone, spare batteries
- Headlamp, first aid, emergency bivy, whistle
- Warm food, thermos, extra water
- PLB/satellite messenger recommended

Overnight winter camping (additions)
- 4‑season tent or well‑anchored winter setup
- Winter sleeping bag (rated below expected low), R≥5 pad or two‑pad system
- Stove suitable for cold (liquid fuel recommended) + extra fuel
- Shovel, repair kit, spare gloves/socks, hand/foot warmers
- Avalanche kit and training if relevant

Final tips
- Test your gear in a local cold day trip before relying on it on a remote trek.
- Keep electronics warm (inside jacket). Rotate wet socks/gloves to dry inside jacket while moving.
- Be conservative with route choice; it’s easier to go home early than to fix a cold emergency.
- Consider hiring a guide or joining a group for your first winter outings.

If you tell me where (region/elevation), how long you plan to be out, and your experience level, I’ll give a tailored gear list and specific route/decision recommendations.', type='output_text', test_results.response:

Below is a prioritized, practical checklist plus brief notes on adjustments for fitness, weather, and emergencies.

Essentials (minimum for a safe summer day hike)
- Pack: 20–30 L daypack with rain cover or dry bags.  
- Water: 2–3 L per person (more in very hot/humid conditions or if terrain is strenuous). Carry a backup: spare bottle or collapsible reservoir.  
- Food: lunch + extra snacks (energy bars, trail mix, sandwiches). Bring at least one extra snack portion beyond planned.  
- Footwear: broken-in hiking shoes or lightweight boots with good traction and ankle support as needed for rocky terrain.  
- Clothing (avoid cotton): moisture-wicking base layer, breathable hiking shorts/pants, light long-sleeve sun shirt, wide-brim hat, sunglasses. Pack a lightweight insulating layer if elevation changes.  
- Rain/lightning protection: lightweight waterproof rain shell (hooded). Summer storms can come fast.  
- Navigation: paper map + compass and a charged phone/GPS with offline maps. Learn to use the paper map/compass before you go.  
- Sun protection: SPF 30+ sunscreen (face and body), SPF lip balm.  
- First-aid kit: basics + blister care (moleskin/compeed), adhesive, antiseptic wipes, pain reliever, antihistamine. Tailor to group size/medical needs.  
- Emergency shelter: emergency bivy or aluminized space blanket (very lightweight). A poncho can double as shelter.  
- Headlamp or small flashlight with spare batteries.  
- Multi-tool or knife, small roll of duct tape or repair kit.  
- Lightweight trekking poles (optional but helpful on descents/steep or loose terrain).  
- Insect repellent and tick removal tool (if ticks/mosquitoes are common).  
- ID, cash, and any personal meds (EpiPen if allergic).  
- Trash bag: pack out all waste, including toilet paper.

Safety & communication
- Tell someone your route, start time, and expected return time. Check in when you’re back.  
- Check weather and trail conditions before leaving; delay or reroute if thunderstorms, extreme heat, or fire closures are forecast.  
- Start early to avoid hottest midday hours and thunderstorms.  
- Pace yourself: expect overall hiking speed ~2–3 mph on moderate terrain; adjust for fitness and pack weight.  
- Know signs of heat illness and treat early: slow down, hydrate, move to shade, cool skin.  
- Stay on marked trails, watch footing on loose rock, and avoid ridge tops/trees during lightning.  
- If in bear country, carry bear spray (read instructions) and store food in vehicle or bear canister when not carrying it.  
- Carry a whistle and know how to signal for help (three blasts = emergency).

Adjustments by experience & fitness
- Inexperienced or lower fitness: choose shorter/routes with frequent bail-out options, bring extra water/food, use trekking poles, wear sturdier boots, carry a larger first-aid kit.  
- Experienced/fit hikers: can lighten gear (ultralight clothing, smaller first-aid kit), but still keep navigation, emergency shelter, water backup, and rain protection.

Backup options / emergency planning
- Plan and note bail-out points (trail junctions, road crossings) and estimated times to each.  
- Carry a small power bank for phone/GPS. Consider a satellite messenger or PLB for remote areas with no cell service.  
- If weather turns bad: turn back early, seek low ground away from lightning, put on rain shell, and use emergency shelter if needed.  
- If you run low on water, ration, rest in shade, and move slowly to conserve fluids; if you expect no water sources on trail, bring all you need or a reliable filter + water purification tablets.

Quick packing checklist (day-of)
- Daypack, water, snacks/lunch, shoes, socks, hat, sunglasses, rain jacket, map+compass, phone+power bank, first-aid, headlamp, sunblock, insect repellent, emergency bivy, whistle, ID.

If you tell me your hiking experience, planned distance/elevation, expected temps, and region (wildlife concerns like bears/ticks), I’ll tailor a precise gear list and safety plan for your trip.', test_results.prompt: I'm planning a 3-day backpacking trip in the mountains in October. What are the most critical safety considerations?
test_results.response:
Response(id='resp_36974f9e76387de1006a4650fef504819091b377d3a7b0a5ee', created_at=1782993151.0, error=None, incomplete_details=None, instructions='You are an expert trail guide for Adventure Works. Provide practical hiking and camping guidance.

When recommending:
- Assess user experience and fitness
- Consider weather and trail conditions  
- Suggest appropriate gear
- Emphasize safety protocols
- Offer backup options

Keep guidance specific, actionable, and safety-focused.', metadata={}, model='gpt-5-mini', object='response', output=[ResponseReasoningItem(id='rs_36974f9e76387de1006a4650ffc3c8819097a2e392bacfd532', summary=[], type='reasoning', content=[], encrypted_content=None, status=None, agent_reference={'type': 'agent_reference', 'name': 'trail-guide', 'version': '8'}, response_id='resp_36974f9e76387de1006a4650fef504819091b377d3a7b0a5ee'), ResponseOutputMessage(id='msg_36974f9e76387de1006a46510937d08190a5f4c0e1a06b8b1d', content=[ResponseOutputText(annotations=[], text='Good question — October in the mountains brings great scenery but also some of the year’s biggest hazards (cold nights, early snow, storms and short days). Below are the most critical safety considerations, with clear actions, gear priorities and backup options. If you want a more tailored plan, tell me: where (range/region), typical elevation, group size, and your experience/fitness level.

Quick questions (so I can tailor advice)
- Where are you hiking (mountain range / nearest town)?
- Max elevation you’ll reach?
- Group size and experience (have you done overnight backpacking/route-finding/above-treeline winter travel)?
- Any medical issues or medications?

Top safety priorities (actionable)
1. Check weather and trip timing
   - Action: Study forecasts at 7 days, 48 hours and 12–24 hours before go-time (Mountain-Forecast, National Weather Service, local ranger). Look at daytime highs, nighttime lows, precipitation & freezing level, and wind gusts.
   - Plan: Expect large diurnal swings; plan for below-freezing nights. If forecast includes heavy precipitation + below-freezing temps at your elevation, strongly consider postponing or moving to lower-elevation route.

2. Shorter daylight / route planning
   - Action: Calculate realistic daily mileage with loaded pack and elevation gain; factor in slower travel in cold/technical terrain. Schedule travel to finish tricky sections well before dusk.
   - Rule of thumb: plan for fewer miles than you think; add margin for weather or delays.

3. Hypothermia / cold injury prevention
   - Action: Sleep system and clothing must handle temps at least 10–20°F (6–11°C) colder than forecast. Use layered clothing (wicking base, insulating mid, waterproof breathable shell).
   - Avoid getting wet (rain, sweat). Change into dry clothes before stopping for long breaks or at camp.
   - Know hypothermia signs and treatment (move to shelter, dry clothing, warm fluids, emergency insulation).

4. Navigation and communication
   - Gear: map, compass (and know how to use them), GPS device or phone with offline maps, and power bank(s).
   - Comms: Bring an emergency communicator (satellite messenger or PLB) if cell service is unreliable. Have an agreed check-in plan with someone at home and a pre-set time to report; if you miss the check-in, they should alert authorities.

5. Water & food redundancy
   - Action: Confirm reliable water sources on route; carry purification (filter/chemical) and treat every source. In cold temps, water can freeze — carry insulated bottles or stow in sleeping bag at night.
   - Bring at least an extra day (24–36 hours) of food and fuel for unexpected delays.

6. Shelter and sleep system
   - Gear: Tent rated for expected winds and possible snow; four-season not always necessary but use a sturdy three-season with solid stakes. Sleeping bag rated for temperatures at least 10°F below expected lows and an insulated sleeping pad (R-value appropriate).
   - Bring an emergency bivy or lightweight shelter for emergencies.

7. Footing / winter-tech considerations
   - Action: October may mean slick leaves, wet rock, early snow/ice at higher elevation. If route crosses high ridges or perennial snow, pack microspikes, crampons, and know how to self-arrest (ice axe) if necessary.
   - Use trekking poles for balance on uneven, leaf-covered, or wet terrain.

   - Action: Bears may still be active. Use bear canister or approved hanging methods. Store food away from sleeping area per local regs.
   - Know local wildlife risks (bears, mountain lions) and carry bear spray if recommended.

9. First aid and group management
   - Gear: Comprehensive first-aid kit tailored to the group and trip length; blister care, tape, wound dressings, pain meds, any personal prescriptions.
   - Protocols: Do buddy checks for signs of hypothermia, AMS, or severe fatigue. Set clear turn-around or bail-out criteria before the trip (e.g., if any member shows AMS, or winds > X, or persistent precipitation + temps < 25°F, bail to lower elevation).

10. Permits, route info, and local conditions
    - Action: Obtain required permits, check trail closures, and contact local ranger station for recent trail/stream/parking conditions and enforcement rules (campfire restrictions, water warnings).

Essentials checklist (prioritized)
- Navigation: map, compass, GPS/phone w/ offline maps, power bank
- Emergency comms: satellite messenger or PLB (recommended)
- Shelter: tent + groundsheet, emergency bivy
- Sleep: sleeping bag (10–20°F margin), insulated sleeping pad
- Clothing: base layers (synthetic/wool), insulating midlayer (fleece/down), waterproof breathable shell, warm hat, insulated jacket, gloves (plus lighter liner), spare socks
- Footwear: sturdy waterproof boots, gaiters, microspikes/crampons (if needed)
- Stove & fuel (test in cold), cookware
- Water: bottles, insulated bottle sleeves, purifier/filter
- Food: 3 days + 1 spare day minimum
- First-aid + blister kit, personal meds
- Headlamp + spare batteries
- Repair kit: duct tape, cord, multi-tool, spare shoelace, tent repair

- Sunscreen, sunglasses, lip balm (UV still strong)

Specific October hazards and how to mitigate
- Early snow/ice at higher elevations: check snow reports; carry traction and ice tools if route may be snowy; if unsure, plan a lower-elevation alternative.
- Rapid weather change/wind: choose sheltered camps (tree line vs ridgeline), stake/secure tent, reduce exposure time on exposed ridges.
- Cold nights leading to frozen water: insulate water bottles and stow in sleeping bag overnight; carry small collapsible insulated bottle.
- Leaf-covered trails and obscured stream crossings: slow down, use poles, and confirm route frequently with map/compass.

Decision/bail criteria (examples to set ahead of time)
- Persistent heavy precipitation + below-freezing temps at planned camp elevation.
- Strong sustained winds or wind gusts over safe limit for your tent (local ranger can advise; generally >40 mph is dangerous).
- Any signs of moderate-to-severe AMS (headache, nausea, confusion) — descend immediately.
- Group member exhaustion or injury that slows progress below safe margins before dark.

Backup options (plan these before you go)
- Lower-elevation alternate route or campground
- Shorter loop or out-and-back itinerary with earlier bail points
- Extra day of food and fuel so you can shelter in place if conditions force delay

Training & preparation
- Do at least one or two loaded day hikes of similar elevation gain before trip.
- Practice setting up tent, using stove, and operating emergency comm device in your backyard/in a car so you’re not learning in the field.
- Review basic first-aid and hypothermia/immersion care.

- Forecast shows a sustained storm with freezing temps at your elevation and no feasible sheltered camp.

- You or a group member aren’t physically prepared to complete planned distances safely.

If you tell me the region, elevation, and your group’s experience, I’ll:

Below is a practical, safety-focused checklist and step-by-step plan you can follow. If you tell me where (region, car vs. backpacking, season) I’ll tailor it.

1) Quick assessment & prep
- Experience: If you’ve never backpacked, do a 4–6 mile day hike with a loaded pack first (15–25% of body weight is typical starting point). For car camping you need less conditioning.
- Fitness: Be able to hike at a steady pace on uneven terrain for several hours and handle stairs/steep sections in training hikes.
- Skills to practice at home: tent pitch, stove operation, water treatment, and packing/shouldering your pack.

2) Planning (2–3+ weeks → last-minute)
- Route & permits: Choose a short, well-maintained trail or established campground. Reserve permits/campsites if required.
- Trail & weather: Check recent trip reports, park service/ranger station, and a reliable forecast (48–72 hours before).
- Let someone know: name, route, expected return time, vehicle location. Leave a paper copy in your car too.

3) Essential gear (basic overnight backpacking; for car camping you can omit ultralight choices)
- Shelter: tent (with footprint), stakes, guy lines; practice set-up.
- Sleep: sleeping bag rated for expected low temps, sleeping pad, pillow or stuff sack.
- Pack: appropriate capacity (40–65L for overnight backpacking).
- Clothing (layering system): base layer (moisture-wicking), insulating layer (fleece/down), waterproof-breathable shell, hat, gloves, extra socks, camp shoes.
- Footwear: broken-in hiking boots or trail shoes.
- Cooking & food: stove + fuel, lighter/matches in waterproof container, pot, spoon, lighter, bear canister if required. Pre-plan easy meals; bring extra snack calories (~500 kcal extra).
- Water: container(s) + treatment (filter, chemical drops, or UV). Plan for at least 2–3 liters/day depending on heat/effort.
- Navigation & communication: map, compass, fully charged phone + power bank; consider satellite messenger/PLB for backcountry with no cell coverage.
- Light & batteries: headlamp (extra batteries) and backup light.
- First aid: small kit tailored to blisters, blood, allergic reactions, OTC meds; include blister treatment.
- Emergency: whistle, emergency blanket/bivy, multi-tool, duct tape/repair kit.
- Hygiene & sanitation: trowel, toilet paper in zip bag, hand sanitizer, trash bags.
- Misc: sun protection (hat, sunglasses, sunscreen), insect repellent, trekking poles (optional but helpful).

4) Food & water specifics
- Meals: breakfast (oatmeal), dinner (dehydrated/pasta), lunch/snacks (sandwiches, granola, nuts, bars). Cook something you’ve tried at home.
- Water sources: research where water is available on route; treat all natural water.
- Extra: pack 1–2 extra meals and extra water purification tablets.

5) Safety & campsite protocol
- Campsite selection: use established sites when possible, avoid low areas that collect water, keep 200 ft from water for sanitation.
- Fires: check local rules; use established fire rings only and fully extinguish. Bring a stove as primary cooking method.
- Food storage: use bear canister or hang food where required. Never keep food in your tent.
- Wildlife: make noise on approach, store food properly, know local wildlife protocols (bears, cougars, snakes).
- Weather hazards: have a plan for storms/hypothermia. Bring insulating layers even in summer nights; know how to recognize/manage hypothermia.
- Navigation & decisions: turn back if weather or team condition worsens; set a turnaround time.
- Emergency plan: know nearest exit, ranger contact, and how to use PLB/satellite device.

6) Day-of and campsite routine
- Day-of: check forecast, pack early, do a gear check (fuel, batteries, permits). Leave trip plan with contact.
- On trail: pace conservatively, hydrate & snack regularly, check map at junctions.
- At camp: set tent on flat durable surface, set up rainfly, treat/store food, set up water/filter before dark, light headlamps, keep a tidy site.
- Night: have a small night kit (headlamp, cozy layer, water bottle, whistle).

7) Backup options & contingencies
- Alternative campsite or bail-out trailhead if main site full or conditions bad.
- Extra day’s food or money to stay in nearby town if you can’t continue.
- Cell/satellite communication plan: phone + power bank; consider renting a satellite messenger if going remote.
- If weather turns severe: descend early, shelter in vehicle or solid structure, avoid exposed ridgelines.

8) Practical tips
- Pack light but don’t skimp on safety items.
- Break in footwear and hike with a loaded pack before the trip.
- Test stove and water filter at home.
- Practice Leave No Trace: pack out trash, minimize campfire impacts, respect wildlife and other campers.
